title: "The Need to End the War": Rubio and Lavrov Hold First Face-to-Face Ukraine Talks in 10 Months in Manila
excerpt: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Russia's Sergey Lavrov met for 35 minutes in Manila — their first in-person Ukraine peace talk in 10 months. What was said, and what was left unresolved?
content:
The top diplomats of the United States and Russia sat down together in Manila on Thursday — a 35-minute meeting that marked the first direct, in-person contact between the two sides since September 2025.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov met on the sidelines of the ASEAN Regional Forum in Pasay, Manila. The meeting was requested by the American side. Neither diplomat made any public statement or took questions from reporters before or after.

The US State Department said the two officials "discussed the U.S.-Russia relationship and the need to end the Russia-Ukraine war." Rubio's stated focus was identifying possible paths toward ending the conflict.

The meeting is part of a sustained effort by President Donald Trump's administration to reach a negotiated settlement in Ukraine. Trump, who returned to the White House in January 2025, has pushed for a mediated end to the war since his first days back in office. Talks have stalled repeatedly due to the distance between Russia's demands and what Ukraine is prepared to accept.

The Manila meeting is the latest in a series of contacts at the US-Russia diplomatic level. The two sides were also expected to discuss the US-Iran conflict — a topic that adds significant complexity to any broader security conversation between Washington and Moscow.

The ASEAN forum in Manila gave both sides a neutral, multilateral setting to meet without the optics of a dedicated bilateral summit. Tight scheduling meant the conversation lasted approximately 35 minutes.

Russia has consistently insisted on conditions for any ceasefire that include Ukrainian territorial concessions and security guarantees that Ukraine and its Western partners have rejected. For Ukraine, still under active bombardment more than four years into the war, the significance of any diplomatic meeting at this level is measured by outcomes — not proximity.
